title: Would you accept a job interview in front of judges and an audience?
description:
In the current global economic environment, youth unemployment is higher than the national average in many countries, as companies are reluctant to take on new staff. According to the United Nations, the global youth unemployment rate rose to 12.4 per cent last year, meaning around 67 million people under 24 can’t find jobs.

Now some companies are staging less conventional recruitment processes that are attracting job applicants and buzz.

We speak with journalist MaryLou Costa about L'Oreal’s Brandstorm competition, which turns recruitment into an X Factor-style competition, with jobs as the prize. The process starts with domestic competitions around the world and culminates in a grand final in Paris.

For the young people involved, is it exciting - or unfair? We hear from Allodya Arofa, a final-year university student who won the national competition in Indonesia, about her experience.

summaryZh: 本集 BBC 節目《What in the World》探討企業透過商業競賽與實作簡報等非傳統方式招募新人的現象，以及這對青年求職者帶來的利弊。在全球 24 歲以下青年失業率高達 12.4% 、約 6700 萬人求職困難的背景下，許多企業開始舉辦類似競賽。記者 Mary-Lou Costa 以萊雅 L'Oréal 的 Brandstorm 競賽為例，說明企業如何評估候選人的團隊合作與領導潛力。印尼參賽學生 Alodya Arofah 表示，競賽提供了寶貴的建立人脈與簡報經驗，對於不擅長傳統履歷面試的求職者亦有幫助；然而，此類競賽也被批評需要付出大量額外時間、偏好外向性格，並無形中提高了初階職缺的求職門檻。
summaryEn: With global youth unemployment rising to 12.4%, companies are increasingly adopting unconventional, competition-based hiring methods to evaluate job applicants. Host Hannah Gelbart speaks with journalist Mary-Lou Costa about recruitment contests like L'Oréal's Brandstorm, which requires young applicants to work in teams and pitch business proposals on stage to win job offers. Indonesian finalist Alodya Arofah shares how the contest offered invaluable networking and feedback that traditional job applications cannot provide. However, the episode also examines the downsides: these demanding competitions require significant unpaid time, tend to favor extroverted personalities, and place an increasingly heavy burden on young job seekers.

vocabulary.example: Imagine going for a job, and instead of just sending in your CV and doing an interview, you've got to compete for it on a stage in front of a panel of judges.
Honestly, it was a very nerve-wracking moment to actually pitch our idea to the judges.
More employers are asking potential hires to take part in all sorts of challenges, pitch ideas, solve problems, and compete against each other.
So the most recent United Nations report found the global youth unemployment rate rose to 12.4% last year.

Now, it is a complicated picture, but some of the factors are that lots of countries are facing slowing economic growth, there are fewer jobs being created, there are geopolitical tensions, and of course technology is changing pretty fast.

So competition for jobs is really tough, and you can understand why many university students and recent grads would be willing to go for these less conventional recruiting processes like the one at L'Oréal.

So you go through multiple rounds, you pitch via video, and so on, and then when you get selected to present on stage, there are various levels of that, so there's a national level that took place in London, and I believe that there were various kind of national levels in different countries across the world, and then the winners of those national levels go on to compete in like a global grand final.
I think they want to know kind of how you work in a team because I guess the idea is that you work in a team of three, so they want to know what you come up with collaboratively.

I get to actually network with a lot of people around the world who actually had like the same passion to act to develop a product, and they have the same passion for like business and also marketing.
Yumi personally came across so well in her enthusiasm for the company, her enthusiasm for the product.
